point: Corrects the premise at the start: a health FSA does not roll over like an HSA. It is use-it-or-lose-it by default (IRS Pub 969), and leftover money is forfeited unless the plan has one of two optional features, a carryover or a grace period (a plan has one or neither, never both). The HSA is the account that truly rolls over. Leaving the money alone risks losing most or all of it, but the answer must not say all $1,900 is certainly lost.

Carryover branch: up to $680 of unused 2026 money carries into the 2027 plan year (20% of the $3,400 2026 health FSA limit; Rev. Proc. 2025-32, Notice 2020-33), and the plan may set a lower cap. At the $680 maximum, $1,900 - $680 = $1,220 is forfeited if nothing is spent, so spending at least $1,220 on expenses incurred by Dec 31, 2026 loses nothing and the other $680 carries toward March; a lower plan cap raises the spend by the difference (e.g. $500 cap: spend $1,400).

Grace period branch: the whole $1,900 can pay for expenses incurred until the plan's grace end, at most the 15th day of the third month after year end, i.e. no later than March 15, 2027 (Notice 2005-42); the plan may set a shorter period. Dental work done on March 16 or later is not covered by 2026 money.
Neither-feature branch: if the plan has no carryover and no grace period, all $1,900 is forfeited unless spent on expenses incurred by Dec 31, 2026.

Tells the person to ask HR or the plan administrator now which feature applies (carryover, grace period or neither), the carryover cap or grace end date, and the run-out deadline for filing 2026 claims. The run-out period adds time to file claims, not to incur new expenses.

Expenses count when the care is provided, not when billed or paid, so prepaying the dentist in December for March work does not help (Pub 969: no advance reimbursement of future or projected expenses); suggests doing any part of the dental work before Dec 31 if possible.

Lists eligible spend-down items (Pub 502, Pub 969), such as dental cleanings, X-rays and fillings; eye exams, glasses, contacts and solution; prescriptions; over-the-counter medicine (no prescription needed for an FSA); menstrual products; bandages and medical supplies; copays and deductibles not reimbursed elsewhere.

Points to the 2027 FSA election at open enrollment (usually happening now) to cover the March dental work, since the uniform coverage rule makes the full annual election available from the first day of the plan year.
